rationale:
Today's slate covers five different body systems: liver and metabolism, muscle, stomach and anaesthesia, kidneys, and new drugs. Every piece names a specific drug, because that's the clearest pattern in our analytics so far.

**Trend mix**
- **Emerging or rising (L1, S1, S3):**
  - L1 is survodutide's SYNCHRONIZE-2 trial (NEJM, 1 Oct). It's emerging, has little competition and suits our headline-decoder format: "13% and still a disappointment?"
  - S1 is a Short cut from L1 to send viewers to the long video.
  - S3 covers the UK study on GLP-1s and anaesthesia. It's rising, and the radar marked it "caution", so the angle is strictly "tell your surgical team and follow their instructions", with no stopping or pausing advice.
- **Evergreen with a timely hook (C1):** semaglutide and kidney disease in type 2 diabetes. It leads with FLOW and adds the new Nature Medicine biopsy trial, reporting its null co-primary results exactly. This repackages a benefits-beyond-weight topic with a named drug and population, as the playbook asks.
- **Myth-bust (S2):** "Does tirzepatide (Mounjaro) burn fat or muscle?" It corrects the overstated "preserves muscle" headline (fat-free mass is not the same as skeletal muscle) and uses the search-question format of our #2 Short.

**Pillars:** research ×2, myths, life-on-glp1 and beyond-weight, so no pillar has more than 2 pieces.

**What I left out and why**
- Retatrutide (peaking) and our recent topics: retatrutide had a long-form and a Short on 09-30, and nails, hair loss, amylin and Foundayo heart safety were all covered within the last 30 days.
- The trevogrumab muscle drug: it would put two muscle pieces on the same day as S2.
- The Medicare Bridge: a good candidate for later this week, closer to Open Enrollment on 15 Oct.

pieces.topic: Survodutide (glucagon + GLP-1 dual agonist) in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes: SYNCHRONIZE-2 Phase 3 (NEJM, 1 Oct 2026, n=752, 76 weeks): up to 13.1% weight loss (highest-dose arm) vs 3.1% on placebo; A1C down up to 1.21 points
pieces.angle: Working title (≤100 chars): 'Survodutide in Type 2 Diabetes: 9.8% vs 3.9% Placebo at 76 Weeks. Why Did Investors Shrug?' Alternative if 13.1% is kept: 'Survodutide's 13.1% in T2D: What It Means (and Why Shares Fell)'. Only use this version if the first 10s immediately says '13.1% is the top dose if people stayed on treatment. Counting everyone, the paper reports 9.8% vs 3.9% on placebo.' First 10s: adults with obesity/overweight AND type 2 diabetes, 76 weeks, both estimands with their own placebo figures (13.1% vs 3.1% if staying on treatment; −9.8% vs −3.9% for everyone randomised, 6.0 mg), and 'investigational, not approved as of Oct 2026'. Give A1C per arm from NEJM (−0.9 / −0.8 vs −0.2 points from 7.4%; add mmol/mol), and mention the 1.21 figure only as the release's 'if stayed on treatment' number. Disappointment: 'Zealand Pharma shares fell about 11% on 1 Oct. Analysts cited tolerability and competition.' This is an investor view, not a clinical verdict. Give tolerability per arm from NEJM: GI AEs 72.8% / 77.7% vs 38.6%, plus vomiting and stopping due to side effects for each arm vs placebo. Explain why weight loss is lower in T2D in every major trial of this class (STEP 2, SURMOUNT-2, TRIUMPH-2), with each trial's estimand, duration and dose labelled as a separate trial with no head-to-head. Liver: 'liver-fat reduction was seen in an earlier substudy; MASH outcome trials are still running.' Nothing changes for people on approved medicines. Close with: 'It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.'
pieces.working_title: Survodutide Lost 13.1% (Top Dose) vs 3.1% Placebo in T2D. Why Did It 'Disappoint'?
pieces.why: A brand-new NEJM Phase 3 trial with 'disappointment' headlines, almost no creator explainers yet, and enough depth for 10+ minutes. A named-drug headline decoder is our best-performing title formula. | fact-check: The topic is real and on-pillar. SYNCHRONIZE-2 was published in NEJM (Survodutide Once Weekly in Adults with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes, https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa2607219) with a Boehringer release dated 1 Oct 2026. But the topic line mixes up estimands. 13.1% vs 3.1% and 'A1C down up to 1.21' are the press release's EFFICACY estimand (if people stayed on treatment). The NEJM abstract reports week-76 weight change of −8.2% (3.6 mg), −9.8% (6.0 mg) and −3.9% (placebo). A1C changed by −0.9 (3.6 mg), −0.8 (6.0 mg) and −0.2 points (placebo) from a baseline of 7.4%, so the best A1C result was NOT in the highest-dose arm. Our rule is to use the paper's number, not the press release's 'up to'. n also needs checking: the release says 755, the topic says 752. Use the NEJM randomised and analysed n. Discontinuation is inconsistent across sources: the release says 18% vs 1.2% on placebo, while news coverage (Fierce, Bloomberg) cites 26% stopping after an adverse event and 39% vomiting. Copy the AE-discontinuation and vomiting rates per arm from the NEJM tables only. GI AEs of 72.8% / 77.7% vs 38.6% are confirmed. The 'disappointment' framing is verifiable: Zealand shares fell about 11–12% on 1 Oct, and analysts pointed to tolerability and competitiveness (Bloomberg, Fierce Biotech). Attribute it to investors and analysts, and don't use the word 'markets' broadly. Sponsor: Boehringer Ingelheim (survodutide licensed from Zealand). Say 'developed by Boehringer Ingelheim with Zealand Pharma' unless NEJM lists Zealand as a funder. Comparators: TRIUMPH-2 is now peer-reviewed (Lancet, 29 Sep 2026, retatrutide −11.9/−16.8/−18.8% vs −5.1% at 80 wk), so it can be included. SURMOUNT-2 and STEP 2 are fine too. Label every figure with its estimand, duration and population, and state that there is no head-to-head comparison. Liver: SYNCHRONIZE-2 itself didn't establish a MASH benefit. Liver-fat data come from a SYNCHRONIZE-1 substudy and from Phase 2 MASH work, and Phase 3 MASH outcomes are still ongoing. Label it that way. Survodutide is investigational and not approved as of Oct 2026 (FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation is not approval).

pieces.topic: Survodutide's 13.1% result in type 2 diabetes, decoded: why weight loss is lower in T2D on every GLP-1-type drug
pieces.angle: Title: 'Survodutide in Type 2 Diabetes: Why 13.1% Didn't Impress Investors #shorts'. Within 10s: '13.1% is the top dose for people who stayed on treatment, vs 3.1% on placebo. Counting everyone, it's about 10% vs 4%.' On-screen qualifier: 'top dose · if stayed on treatment · 76 wks · adults with T2D + obesity/overweight · investigational, not approved as of Oct 2026'. Key idea: in every major trial of this drug class so far, people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight than people without it. Only compare against T2D trials (e.g. tirzepatide SURMOUNT-2, retatrutide TRIUMPH-2), labelled as separate trials with no head-to-head. Attribute the 'disappointment' to investors: 'Zealand shares fell about 11%. Analysts pointed to side effects.' One line: 'stomach side effects in about 3 in 4 vs about 4 in 10 on placebo, mostly mild to moderate.' Point viewers to the full video. Close with: 'It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.' 35–50s.
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. A headline decoder that names the drug while the news is fresh drives traffic to the long-form video. | fact-check: Same estimand problem as L1. 13.1% vs 3.1% is the efficacy estimand ('if people stayed on treatment'). NEJM's headline figures are −9.8% (6.0 mg) / −8.2% (3.6 mg) vs −3.9% placebo at 76 weeks. A 13.1% stat pill without its estimand breaks the 'verified number, not press-release up to' rule. 'Lower on every drug in this class' is too absolute. The trial pattern is consistent (STEP 2 vs STEP 1, SURMOUNT-2 vs SURMOUNT-1, SYNCHRONIZE-2 vs SYNCHRONIZE-1, TRIUMPH-2), but say 'in every major trial so far'. 'Markets shrugged' must be attributed: Zealand shares fell about 11% on 1 Oct, with analysts citing tolerability (Bloomberg, Fierce Biotech). The GI rate is confirmed: 72.8–77.7% vs 38.6% on placebo.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) body composition: fat mass −35.4%, fat-free mass −5.1%, skeletal muscle mass stable at 24 weeks (real-world, single-arm, J Diabetes Complications)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Burn Fat or Muscle? What a 24-Week Study Shows #shorts'. Answer within 10s: 'In this real-world study of 122 adults with overweight or obesity (no type 2 diabetes), most of the weight lost was fat: fat mass down 35.4%, fat-free mass down 5.1%. Estimated muscle mass stayed about the same.' On-screen: 'retrospective · no control group · completers only · 24 wks · Italy · body scan by bioimpedance'. Explain that fat-free mass includes water, organs and bone, and that bioimpedance only estimates muscle. Then anchor: 'In the larger SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition), about a quarter of the weight lost was lean mass.' Close: protein at each meal, unless your clinician has told you to limit protein (for example, kidney disease), plus strength training. Then: 'It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.' Present this as 'what it shows and its limits', not 'myth busted'. 35–50s.
pieces.working_title: Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Burn Fat or Muscle? 24-Week Data #shorts
pieces.why: A contrarian-but-true correction of an overstated headline in the search-question format of our #2 Short ('Does Mounjaro speed up metabolism?'). It's a different angle from the 09-28 muscle carousel. | fact-check: The source is real: Brancato D et al., 'Real-world effectiveness of 6-month tirzepatide therapy on body weight and composition in adults with overweight and obesity', J Diabetes Complications 2026;40(11):109419, doi:10.1016/j.jdiacomp.2026.109419. Details: retrospective, no control arm, n=122, two centres in Palermo, Italy, 79.5% female, people with type 2 diabetes and prior GLP-1 users excluded, treatment completers only, body composition by bioelectrical impedance (BIA). Fat mass −35.4%, fat-free mass −5.1%, skeletal muscle mass 'remained stable'. Framing problem: the angle calls it a 'myth-bust of tirzepatide preserves muscle', but this paper itself reports stable skeletal muscle. Calling it a myth would contradict the source. Being a small, completers-only BIA study doesn't make it false, so it's 'not proven', not 'a myth'. The honest angle is 'what this study can and can't tell you'. Key limits to state: BIA estimates muscle and is sensitive to hydration, completers only, no control group, mostly women, no people with T2D. Also note that a separate small US real-world BIA study (Frontiers in Endocrinology 2026, n=35, about 81 weeks) reported skeletal muscle mass down 8.3%, so findings vary. Anchor to the SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy (adults with BMI 30+, or 27+ with a weight-related condition, without diabetes): about three-quarters of the weight lost was fat and about a quarter was lean mass. Copy the exact figures from the paper. Tirzepatide is the generic name, and Zepbound/Mounjaro are for recognition only.

pieces.topic: GLP-1 medicines and anaesthesia: regurgitation or aspiration in 1.41% of GLP-1 users vs 0.12% of non-users (UK prospective observational cohort, 47,039 patients, 119 sites, Anaesthesia)
pieces.angle: Title: 'GLP-1 Meds Like Semaglutide & Anesthesia: 1.41% vs 0.12% in UK Study #shorts' (or 'Taking Semaglutide or Tirzepatide Before Surgery? What a UK Study Found'). First line: 'On a GLP-1 medicine like semaglutide or tirzepatide and having surgery or an endoscopy? Tell your anaesthetist.' Mechanism: slower stomach emptying can leave food in the stomach. Numbers: among 1,348 people who had used a GLP-1 medicine in the previous 3 months, 19 had regurgitation or aspiration (17 regurgitation, 2 aspiration): 1.41%, vs 0.12% of everyone else (about 1 in 71 vs 1 in 802). On-screen: 'observational · linked to, not proof · UK hospitals · GLP-1 users were more likely to have obesity/diabetes'. Guidance: 'Professional guidance differs, so your surgical team decides the plan.' Only action: tell your surgical and anaesthesia team and follow their instructions. Never say stop, pause or keep taking it on your own. Close with: 'It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.' 35–50s.
pieces.working_title: Semaglutide (Ozempic) & Anesthesia: 1.41% vs 0.12% Regurgitation in UK Study #shorts
pieces.why: A high-intent search ('stop Ozempic before surgery') with a fresh prospective study. The radar marked it caution, so the angle is limited to 'tell your team', which is safe and genuinely useful. | fact-check: Verified: Potter TE et al., 'Peri-operative glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and outcomes: a national prospective multicentre cohort study', Anaesthesia 2026. 47,039 patients, 119 UK sites, 1,348 GLP-1 RA users (2.9%). 19 events (17 regurgitation, 2 aspiration) = 1.41% vs 57/45,691 = 0.12% (OR 11.39; about 1 in 71 vs 1 in 802). GLP-1 use was defined as use within 3 months before the procedure. The authors say causality can't be determined: obesity and diabetes, both aspiration risk factors, were more common in the GLP-1 group, and events may have been under-reported. That confounding caveat must be on screen or in the narration. The Association of Anaesthetists recommends continuing GLP-1 RAs peri-operatively, while other societies' guidance has differed, so the 'your team decides' framing is right. Never tell viewers to stop, pause or continue on their own. Title problem: the study covered all GLP-1 RAs, not semaglutide or Ozempic specifically. Leading with 'Semaglutide (Ozempic)' implies a drug-specific result the study didn't report. Name the class first, with examples.

pieces.topic: Semaglutide and kidney disease in type 2 diabetes: FLOW outcomes plus the new Nature Medicine mechanistic RCT (biopsy + MRI, n=33)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Semaglutide & Kidney Disease in Type 2 Diabetes: What FLOW and a New Biopsy Study Show'. Slide 2 FLOW: adults with T2D + CKD, semaglutide 1.0 mg weekly vs placebo, 24% lower risk of major kidney events (HR 0.76), with absolute events from the paper (331 vs 410) and median follow-up of about 3.4 years. Qualifier line plus source tag. Slide 4 REMODEL (Nature Medicine 2026): '106 adults with T2D + CKD, 52 weeks, randomised vs placebo. The main MRI measures (kidney oxygen, blood flow, inflammation) showed no significant difference vs placebo.' Slide 5: 'In a biopsy subgroup of 33: signs of less fibrosis progression and lower vascular resistance · secondary/exploratory · small · hypothesis.' Slide 6: each route tagged to the source that states it. Slide 7: ask about eGFR, urine albumin (UACR), and how semaglutide fits with SGLT2 inhibitors and your other kidney medicines. No switching advice. Close with: 'It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.' The caption opens with kidney-health/mechanism framing, with no 'weight loss' or brand names before the fold.
pieces.working_title: Semaglutide & Kidney Disease in Type 2 Diabetes: What FLOW and a New Biopsy Trial Show
pieces.why: An evergreen benefits-beyond-weight topic refreshed by the 1 Oct Nature Medicine paper. It names the drug and population as the playbook asks, competition is low, and it's a framework people will save. | fact-check: Both sources exist. FLOW (Perkovic et al., NEJM 2024): adults with T2D and CKD, semaglutide 1.0 mg vs placebo, 24% lower risk of the primary kidney composite (HR 0.76; 331 vs 410 events; median follow-up about 3.4 years; stopped early for efficacy). Copy the absolute rates exactly from the paper. The topic has a scope error on the Nature Medicine trial (REMODEL, 'Effects of semaglutide on kidney disease in type 2 diabetes: a randomized placebo-controlled trial', https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04674-2). REMODEL enrolled 106 participants across 8 countries over 52 weeks. n=33 was the BIOPSY subgroup, not the whole trial (single-nucleus transcriptomics n=22, spatial n=13). The co-primary MRI outcomes (oxygenation by R2*, perfusion, T1 inflammation) showed no significant difference vs placebo. Report those with the MRI-analysed n, not 33. The 'less fibrosis progression' and 'vascular resistance' findings must be labelled secondary/exploratory, from a small subgroup, and hypothesis-generating. Each mechanism route on slide 6 needs a source that actually says it. FLOW and the REMODEL paper discuss blood pressure, glycaemia, inflammation and weight. Slide 7 SGLT2 question: FLOW has a published analysis showing the effect was consistent with or without SGLT2 inhibitors (Mann et al., Nat Med 2024), which can be cited. No switching advice. Semaglutide in FLOW was Ozempic (1.0 mg). Don't name Wegovy.
